meta.title: Who really said "But the best evidence we have that time travel is not possible, and never will be, is that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine. Hawking said it in a January 1991 Darwin lecture at Cambridge, printed as “The Future of the Universe” in Black Holes and Baby Universes (1993).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'But the best evidence we have that time travel is not possible, and never will be, is that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified word for word: a January 1991 Cambridge lecture, collected in Black Holes and Baby Universes. His 1992 Physical Review D paper words it differently.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1942–2018 · theoretical physicist; Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, Cambridge, 1979–2009
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed word for word in Hawking’s essay “The Future of the Universe,” which the book footnotes as a Darwin lecture given at the University of Cambridge in January 1991 and prints as essay 13 of Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays (Bantam Press, 1993). He made the same joke, more drily, in the closing line of his 1992 Physical Review D paper “Chronology protection conjecture.”

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Darwin lecture given at the University of Cambridge, January 1991
Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays
Bantam Press, London & New York, 1993 — essay 13, beginning p. 127

source.excerpt: Perhaps fortunately for our survival (and that of our mothers), it seems that the laws of physics do not allow such time travel. There seems to be a Chronology Protection Agency that makes the world safe for historians by preventing travel into the past. … The Chronology Protection Hypothesis is supported by some recent calculations that I and other people have done. But the best evidence we have that time travel is not possible, and never will be, is that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future.
trail: January 1991 — Hawking delivers “The Future of the Universe” as a Darwin lecture at the University of Cambridge, closing a passage about a “Chronology Protection Agency” with this sentence (Quote Investigator ↗).
28 January 1992 — the Chicago Tribune runs the line in its “Quotes of the Day” column, dropping the opening “But” — the clipped form most reposts still use (Quote Investigator ↗).

15 July 1992 — Hawking puts the joke through peer review. The closing sentence of “Chronology protection conjecture” in Physical Review D reads “There is also strong experimental evidence in favor of the conjecture from the fact that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future” (Quote Investigator ↗, transcribing p. 610).

1993 — the lecture is printed as essay 13 of Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays, with the footnote naming the January 1991 Darwin lecture; the collection’s contents list is on the Internet Archive catalog record ↗.
source.excerptNote: From essay 13, “The Future of the Universe.” The famous sentence is the punchline of the paragraph: Hawking sets out the physics he thinks forbids travel into the past, then offers the empty tourist trade as the clincher.

author.name: Stephen Hawking
author.heading: About Stephen Hawking
author.metaLine: 1942–2018 · English theoretical physicist; Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge, 1979–2009
author.bio: Stephen Hawking worked on black holes, singularities and the quantum structure of spacetime, and held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1979 to 2009. A Brief History of Time (1988) made him the most recognisable physicist alive, and the deadpan one-liner was one of his standard instruments — the 1992 journal paper in which he argued that the universe forbids time machines ends by calling the absence of visitors “strong experimental evidence.” The same 1993 collection that carries this quotation also contains his essay “My Experience with ALS.”

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong book — and usually the wrong words
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound: this really is Hawking. What travels badly is the wording and the source. The line is routinely pinned to the wrong book, quoted with its first word amputated, or replaced altogether by a snappier sentence he does not appear to have written.

items.scope: “If time travel is possible, where are the tourists from the future?”
items.who: Credited to Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time
items.why: This tightened rhetorical question is what most quote sites serve up — Goodreads ↗ attributes it to A Brief History of Time. The wormholes-and-time-travel chapter of that book does discuss the absence of visitors, but in different words; the question form is a later compression, not a sentence of Hawking’s that anyone has produced.

The famous sentence is often footnoted to Hawking’s journal article. The article’s actual closing line is drier: “There is also strong experimental evidence in favor of the conjecture from the fact that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future” — transcribed from p. 610 by Quote Investigator ↗.

Hawking’s sentence begins “But the best evidence…” because it follows a paragraph of actual physics about the Chronology Protection Hypothesis. The Chicago Tribune printed it without the “But” in its “Quotes of the Day” column on 28 January 1992, and that decapitated version is the one that circulates (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quote Investigator notes the phrase itself turns up in Silverberg’s 1968 novel — but without Hawking’s argument that the absence of such tourists is evidence against time travel. The phrase predates him; the joke does not (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Hawking’s own wording, in full: “But the best evidence we have that time travel is not possible, and never will be, is that we have not been invaded by hordes of tourists from the future” — from “The Future of the Universe,” a Darwin lecture given at the University of Cambridge in January 1991 and printed in Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why a physicist reached for a joke
lead: Hawking was not only being flippant. By the early 1990s time travel had briefly become a respectable research topic: his own paper opens by noting the suggestion that “an advanced civilization might have the technology to warp spacetime so that closed timelike curves would appear,” and it works through cosmic strings, Cauchy horizons and the energy-momentum tensor before answering with the chronology protection conjecture — the proposal that the laws of physics step in to stop a time machine ever switching on.

The tourists line is what happens when a physicist reaches for the one piece of evidence a lay audience already holds. In the lecture he called it simply the best evidence we have; in the journal he upgraded it to “strong experimental evidence.” Eighteen years later he ran the experiment properly, throwing a party for time travellers at Gonville and Caius College on 28 June 2009 and posting the invitations only afterwards, so that nobody without a time machine could have known. Nobody came (Wikipedia ↗).
context.detailsSummary: Why ‘experimental evidence’ is a joke told with a straight face
detailsBody: The argument is the Fermi paradox pointed down the time axis rather than across space: if the thing were possible, where is everybody? Hawking never pretended it was a proof. In the 1992 paper it arrives after nine pages of Cauchy horizons and energy-momentum tensors, as the very last sentence of the body before the acknowledgements.

The standard objections write themselves: a time machine can only carry you back as far as the moment it was switched on, so an era before the first machine would see no tourists at all — and visitors who could warp spacetime could presumably also avoid being noticed. Hawking’s serious case rested on the calculations, not on the empty tourist trade.
context.pull: There seems to be a Chronology Protection Agency that makes the world safe for historians by preventing travel into the past.

Hawking's time traveller party was held 28 June 2009 at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge; invitations were sent only after the party ended so that only a time traveller could have attended, and no one arrived.

Stephen Hawking was born 8 January 1942, died 14 March 2018, was English, held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1979 to 2009, and conjectured that travel into the past is effectively impossible.
Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays is a 1993 collection of essays, interviews and talks by Stephen Hawking published by the Bantam Dell Publishing Group.
